services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin handles AC repair in Austin, TX, including warm air, water leaks, unusual noises, and thermostat or condenser faults. Call (512) 635-7760.
services.blurb: Warm air, water leaks, noises, and other AC faults checked in Austin.

paragraphs: Warm air from the supply vents, a rattling sound at the outdoor unit, a damp patch below the air handler, or an electric bill that climbs while the thermostat setting stays the same are all signs that an AC component needs attention. We trace the fault through the thermostat, indoor equipment, condenser, wiring, drain line, and refrigerant circuit rather than treating every no-cooling call as the same problem.

A system may run constantly without lowering the room temperature when a capacitor is weak, a contactor is worn, a blower motor is struggling, or the refrigerant charge is outside the equipment specifications. Water around the indoor cabinet can come from a blocked condensate drain, a frozen evaporator coil, or a cracked drain pan. A clicking breaker, burnt odor, or buzzing electrical compartment calls for a different check than a unit that simply has weak airflow at one register.

AC repair should not wait when there is a burning smell, repeated breaker trip, water escaping from the drain pan, ice on the refrigerant line, or no cooling during hot weather. Those conditions can damage the compressor, ceiling material, wiring, or coil if the unit continues to run.

sections.heading: Warm air and water leaks
paragraphs: Customers often call us because the AC is blowing warm air, the outside unit is humming but the fan is not turning, the thermostat screen is blank, or water is dripping through a ceiling near the indoor unit. Other common descriptions include a loud bang when the condenser starts, a grinding blower sound, short cycling every few minutes, and one bedroom that never reaches the thermostat setting. Each symptom points us toward different components, from a capacitor or fan motor to a control board, float switch, drain trap, or refrigerant leak.

A warm vent does not identify one failed part, and a puddle beneath the air handler does not always mean the drain line alone is blocked. We inspect the equipment and take readings before recommending a repair, because faults that look alike from the room can require very different parts and labor.

sections.heading: Condenser and air-handler inspection
paragraphs: At a repair call, we start with the thermostat setting, return-air temperature, supply-air temperature, filter condition, breaker, disconnect, and visible wiring. We inspect the condenser fan, contactor, capacitor, compressor terminals, indoor blower, evaporator cabinet, condensate pan, safety switches, and drain route. We use a meter to check the 24-volt control circuit and component readings, and we take refrigerant pressure and temperature measurements when the sealed system needs evaluation.

Initial electrical and airflow checks commonly take 20 to 30 minutes, while a refrigerant diagnosis or an intermittent control fault can take longer because the system must run through a cooling cycle. Items such as a capacitor, contactor, float switch, clogged drain line, or accessible wiring connection can often be handled during the same visit when the correct part is available. A failed compressor, leaking coil, damaged circuit board, or part that must be ordered may require a return appointment after the equipment and replacement part are confirmed.

sections.heading: Capacitor access and circuit boards
paragraphs: The part that has failed is a major factor in the repair scope. An accessible capacitor or contactor in the condenser compartment is a different job from a compressor electrical failure, an evaporator coil leak, or a circuit board with heat damage. Older equipment can also have discontinued controls or matching parts that need to be located before work is scheduled.

Access changes the work as well. A condenser behind a locked gate, an air handler in a tight attic, a drain line routed through a wall, or a control board behind a sealed panel adds time for safe entry and testing. If a specific motor, board, coil, or factory control has to be ordered, we confirm the model and part match before the repair is completed.

sections.heading: Model plate and thermostat
paragraphs: Before calling, check the thermostat display and note whether the indoor blower, outdoor condenser fan, or neither unit is running. The model and serial plate is usually on the side of the outdoor condenser or inside the air-handler cabinet, and a clear photo helps us identify the correct capacitor, motor, board, or refrigerant information.

Tell us which room has warm vents, where water is appearing, and whether a breaker has tripped or the equipment is making a new sound. If the air handler is in an attic, garage closet, or ceiling space, let us know about the access opening and any stored items around the panel. Have the filter size available if you know it, since a restricted filter can affect airflow and coil temperature. Call Air Conditioning Austin at (512) 635-7760; a blocked drain or frozen coil can worsen into water damage or compressor strain when the system keeps running.

services.name: AC Tune-Up
services.title: AC Tune-Up | Air Conditioning Austin | Austin, TX
services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin provides AC tune-up checks in Austin, TX, including filters, coils, electrical parts, drainage, and thermostat operation.
services.blurb: AC tune-up checks for filters, coils, controls, and drainage in Austin.

paragraphs: A routine tune-up and an air conditioner that has stopped cooling can both begin with a warm hallway or a thermostat that will not hold the set temperature, but they are not the same visit. A system that still cools steadily, starts normally, and has no water around the indoor unit is usually due for maintenance. Warm supply vents, repeated shutoffs, a tripped breaker, or a puddle by the air handler point to a fault that needs to be found during the check.

We handle both situations at Air Conditioning Austin. We inspect the outdoor condenser, indoor air handler, return grille, filter slot, thermostat, drain line, and electrical connections to determine whether the equipment needs routine adjustment or whether a worn component is affecting cooling.

A planned tune-up can usually wait for a convenient visit when the AC is operating normally, because its purpose is to catch dirt, drainage restrictions, and weakening electrical parts before a breakdown. A unit that is blowing warm air, leaking water, or cycling off repeatedly should not be left running, since a blocked drain, frozen coil, or failing control can worsen while the system continues to run.

sections.heading: Warm air and loud clicking
paragraphs: “My AC is running but the air is warm” is one of the most common calls for a tune-up check. The cause may be a clogged filter restricting airflow, a dirty outdoor coil releasing heat poorly, a thermostat setting issue, or a component that needs closer testing.

Customers also report loud clicking at the condenser, a fan that starts and stops, water near the indoor cabinet, or a musty smell when air comes through the supply vents. Clicking can involve a contactor or capacitor, while water often traces back to the condensate pan, drain line, or an iced evaporator coil.

Other useful symptoms include a room that stays warmer than the rest of the house, weak air from one register, short cooling cycles, and a thermostat display that goes blank. Each symptom can come from more than one part, and faults that sound alike from the hallway can require very different work and parts once we inspect the equipment.

sections.heading: Cooling system inspection
paragraphs: During a cooling system inspection, we begin at the thermostat and confirm the call for cooling, temperature response, and fan operation. We inspect the filter, return path, supply vents, indoor coil area, condensate pan, drain connection, blower compartment, outdoor coil, disconnect, and visible wiring.

We measure temperature change across the system and check operating readings against the equipment specifications. The refrigerant circuit is not judged by one universal pressure because pressure changes with the refrigerant type, outdoor temperature, indoor load, and equipment design. We also check capacitor readings, contactor condition, electrical connections, drain flow, and signs of oil or water around the equipment.

A standard inspection commonly takes about 30 to 60 minutes for one accessible system, with more time needed when the air handler is in a tight attic, the filter cabinet is difficult to reach, or the coil and drain need additional cleaning. Filter replacement, drain clearing, thermostat adjustments, and minor accessible corrections are often handled during the visit when the needed material is available. A failed motor, control board, coil, or other ordered component is documented and scheduled for a separate return visit.

sections.heading: Filter access and control parts
paragraphs: The system age matters because older condensers and air handlers may use parts that are no longer carried as common stock. A capacitor, contactor, blower control, or thermostat component that must be matched to the model can add ordering time compared with a filter or drain-line service.

Access also changes the work involved. An air handler behind a low attic opening, a condenser enclosed by shrubs, or a filter rack that cannot slide out without moving a panel takes more labor than equipment with clear working space.

The condition of the drain line, coil, disconnect, and electrical terminals affects the scope as well. A drain that clears normally is different from a line with standing water, and a disconnect or connection that is heat-damaged needs more attention than a clean, accessible component. If an electrical correction or equipment alteration requires outside approval, that requirement is discussed before related work moves forward.

sections.heading: Model plate and air handler
paragraphs: Before you call, check the model number on the equipment plate, usually found on the side of the outdoor condenser or inside the air-handler cabinet door. The model and serial label helps us identify the correct filter size, electrical components, and manufacturer-specific controls.

Let us know which room has the warmest supply vent, whether the thermostat screen is on, and whether the outdoor fan is running. It also helps to mention water at the drain pan, ice on the refrigerant line, a breaker that has tripped, or a filter that looks dark with dust.

Tell us where the indoor unit is located and whether there is clear access to the attic hatch, closet, garage, or utility room. Call Air Conditioning Austin at (512) 635-7760, because a blocked drain, dirty coil, or weakening capacitor can turn a maintenance issue into a cooling shutdown if it waits.

services.name: Air Conditioner Replacement
services.h1: Air Conditioner Replacement in Austin, TX
services.title: AC Replacement | Air Conditioning Austin | Austin, TX
services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin handles air conditioner replacement in Austin, TX, with equipment checks, sizing review, access planning, and clear next steps.
services.blurb: We replace aging and failed air conditioning systems across Austin and nearby areas.

paragraphs: When an air conditioner changes from an annoyance to a problem, the change is usually visible in the house before the system stops entirely. We see bedrooms that stay warm after the thermostat reaches its setting, supply vents that blow weakly, and condenser units that run through the afternoon without bringing the indoor temperature down. Over a week, the system may run longer and cycle more often. Over a month, a struggling compressor, blower motor, or refrigerant circuit can add wear to components that were already near the end of their service life.

We also see aging systems reach a point where one repair exposes the next weak part. A leak in an older evaporator coil, a failing compressor, or an obsolete control board can leave a homeowner deciding between another temporary repair and a new matched system. If the outdoor condenser and indoor air handler are not matched for capacity and refrigerant type, replacing only one piece may not be the right route.

We start by looking at the equipment, the duct connections, the electrical disconnect, and the rooms the system serves so we can discuss replacement based on the condition in front of us. A replacement can sometimes be planned when the unit is still cooling consistently, but a system that has stopped cooling, trips breakers, or has a compressor failure should not be left through a hot Austin season because indoor heat and extended run time will keep getting worse.

sections.heading: Warm air and loud noises
paragraphs: We hear calls about an AC that is blowing warm air, especially when the thermostat is set lower but the supply registers never feel cool. Warm air can come from a refrigerant issue, a failed compressor, a condenser fan problem, a frozen evaporator coil, or an indoor blower that is not moving enough air across the coil. We check the indoor and outdoor equipment before treating warm air as a reason to replace the whole system.

We also hear descriptions such as a loud buzzing outside, a grinding sound from the closet, a rattle at startup, or a click followed by no cooling. A buzzing condenser can point to an electrical component or compressor problem, while grinding at the air handler can involve a blower motor or wheel. Metal-on-metal noise, repeated breaker trips, and a compressor that tries but cannot start deserve a closer inspection rather than continued cycling.

Other replacement calls begin with water around the air handler, ice on the refrigerant line, a burning odor at a vent, or one side of the home that is much warmer than the rest. A clogged drain, airflow restriction, electrical fault, duct issue, and failing coil can produce overlapping symptoms. We sort out the equipment fault because the same warm room or loud unit can lead to very different parts, labor, and replacement decisions.

sections.heading: Equipment inspection
paragraphs: At an equipment inspection, we record the model and serial data from the condenser and air handler, check the thermostat operation, inspect the disconnect and breaker, and look over the refrigerant line set, condensate drain, filter slot, and visible duct connections. We also compare the temperature at return and supply registers, listen to the compressor and blower, and check whether the cabinet, coil, or wiring shows heat damage or corrosion.

A replacement survey commonly takes about 30 to 60 minutes, depending on whether the air handler is in an attic, closet, garage, or tight crawlspace. We measure the equipment cabinet, the return opening, the supply plenum, and the route for moving an old unit out and a new unit in. We also check the outdoor pad, line-set path, electrical connection, and clearance around the condenser.

During that visit, we can usually confirm the existing system type, document access conditions, and identify visible work such as a new pad, drain safety switch, disconnect, or transition piece at the ductwork. The actual equipment replacement is normally scheduled separately because the selected condenser, air handler or furnace, coil, and any required materials need to be matched and available. If an electrical upgrade, permit, or inspection sign-off applies, we include that requirement in the scope before installation work begins.

sections.heading: Equipment age and attic access
paragraphs: The age and condition of the condenser, coil, and air handler move the scope because older equipment may use discontinued parts or an older refrigerant setup that does not match current replacement equipment. We check the rating plate, the condition of the coil cabinet, and whether the indoor and outdoor sections can be replaced as a properly matched system. A unit with a readable model plate and standard connections is usually simpler to identify than equipment with missing labels, altered wiring, or previous nonstandard modifications.

Access changes the work as well. We account for attic stairs, ceiling openings, narrow hallways, closet doors, platform height, and the path between the air handler and the exterior. An attic unit behind a small access opening may require more preparation than a garage air handler with clear floor space, and a condenser set behind a gate or close to landscaping can affect removal and placement.

The refrigerant line set, electrical disconnect, condensate drain, duct transition, and permit requirements can also affect the final scope. We inspect whether the line set can be reused safely, whether the drain has proper routing, and whether the electrical components are suitable for the replacement equipment. If a required component must be ordered or an inspection sign-off is needed, those items are identified before the replacement is scheduled.

sections.heading: Model plate and air handler
paragraphs: Before calling, we ask that you look for the model number on the metal rating plate of the outdoor condenser and, if accessible, the indoor air handler or furnace cabinet. We can use a clear photo of that label to identify the equipment family, refrigerant type, and approximate age. Let us know which rooms stay warm, whether the system is running now, and whether the thermostat displays an error or keeps calling for cooling. Tell us if the air handler is in an attic, closet, garage, or crawlspace, and whether there is a narrow stairway, gate, or ceiling opening on the access route. Call Air Conditioning Austin at (512) 635-7760 before a failed condenser or overheated indoor space turns a single warm room into a house that cannot cool.

services.name: Air Conditioner Installation
services.h1: Air Conditioner Installation in Austin, TX
services.title: AC Installation | Air Conditioning Austin | Austin, TX
services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin installs central AC systems in Austin, TX, with checks of equipment size, ducts, line sets, drains, electrical service, and access.
services.blurb: We install properly sized AC systems for homes across Austin and nearby areas.

paragraphs: Turning the thermostat lower, replacing a clogged filter, and checking the breaker are sensible first steps when a house feels warm. A blocked filter can reduce airflow at the supply registers, and a tripped breaker can stop the outdoor condenser without warning. Those checks have limits, though: they cannot correct an undersized system, a failed compressor, a leaking evaporator coil, or equipment that has reached the end of its workable life.

We look at the whole cooling setup rather than treating the outdoor unit as the only part that matters. The condenser, indoor coil, blower, return duct, condensate drain, line set, disconnect box, and thermostat all need to suit the home and work together. Installing a larger unit without checking the return air path or duct capacity can leave rooms unevenly cooled and can make the system cycle too quickly.

A planned air conditioner installation can wait long enough for a proper survey when the existing system still cools, because equipment size, electrical connections, and drain routing need to be matched before replacement. A system that will not run should not be left through rising outdoor temperatures, especially when a stalled condenser or overflowing drain is already affecting the home.

sections.heading: AC won't cool or keeps running
paragraphs: Customers often call because the AC will not cool, warm air is coming from the vents, or the outdoor unit will not start while the indoor blower still runs. Other common descriptions include a system that keeps running without lowering the room temperature, a breaker that trips when the condenser starts, water around the air handler, or a burning-plastic smell near the electrical disconnect.

Those symptoms can point to very different parts: a capacitor, contactor, compressor, blower motor, evaporator coil, drain pan, refrigerant line, or breaker. Some faults can be isolated to a component, while others show that the existing equipment no longer makes sense to keep in service. The sound from the condenser or the temperature at one register cannot establish the scope by itself, and each possible fault carries a different amount of labor, material, and equipment work.

sections.heading: In-home equipment survey
paragraphs: During an in-home equipment survey, we inspect the existing condenser and indoor unit, read the model plate, and measure the rooms, return grille, supply vents, equipment closet, pad, line set route, drain connection, and electrical disconnect. We also check the breaker panel, the voltage supplied to the condenser, duct condition, ceiling or attic access, and the location of windows that add heat to a room. A survey commonly takes about 30 to 60 minutes, depending on whether the air handler is in a closet, attic, garage, or crawlspace.

We can usually complete the measurements, equipment review, and installation planning during that visit. If the project calls for a new condenser, indoor coil or air handler, line set, pad, disconnect, or duct alteration, the installation is scheduled after the equipment and any required permit items are arranged. A straightforward changeout can often take a full day, while a new line set route, difficult attic access, or duct changes may require another scheduled workday.

sections.heading: Line sets and panel access
paragraphs: The existing line set and its route can change the scope considerably. A clean, accessible line set of the correct size is different from copper tubing that is kinked, buried in a wall, corroded, or routed through a tight attic. If the tubing cannot be reused, the route from the indoor coil to the outdoor pad has to be planned around walls, framing, insulation, and finished surfaces.

Electrical service and equipment access also matter. A ground-level condenser beside an open gate is a different installation from a unit on a roof, behind a locked enclosure, or above a steep stairway. An older breaker panel, a seized disconnect, a damaged condenser pad, altered ductwork, equipment that must be ordered, or permit sign-off can all add steps before a new system can be put into operation.

sections.heading: Model plate and access path
paragraphs: Before calling, check the model number on the metal plate of the outdoor condenser and, if you can reach it safely, the label on the indoor air handler or furnace cabinet. Let us know which rooms stay warm, whether the system is cooling at all, and whether the breaker trips or the thermostat display is blank. It also helps to describe the equipment location, such as an attic, closet, garage, roof, or side yard, and any gate, stairway, or narrow hallway on the access path. A photo of the condenser, disconnect box, and equipment closet can help us plan the right installation scope. Call Air Conditioning Austin at (512) 635-7760 before a non-running condenser leaves the house without cooling or a condensate overflow damages ceiling drywall.

services.name: Duct Repair
services.title: Duct Repair | Air Conditioning Austin | Austin, TX
services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin handles duct leaks, loose runs, crushed flex duct, and disconnected vents in Austin, TX. Tell us the room, vent, and attic access.
services.blurb: Duct repairs for loose, leaking, crushed, or disconnected runs in Austin.

paragraphs: We hear from homeowners who say one bedroom is always hot, the air barely comes out of a ceiling vent, or the house feels dusty whenever the blower starts. Those are everyday descriptions of ductwork trouble: a loose connection, a split flex duct, a crushed run, an open return, or insulation that has pulled away from the duct.

We also get calls about a rattling sound above a hallway ceiling, a vent that suddenly stopped blowing, or cool air pouring into an attic instead of a living room. A duct run carries conditioned air between the air handler and each register, so a gap at a collar or a damaged section can affect one room while the rest of the system appears normal.

A duct repair should not wait when a room has little airflow, a return is pulling attic dust, or a disconnected run is dumping cooled air outside the living space. The longer a damaged duct stays open, the more conditioned air, insulation performance, and blower capacity are wasted.

sections.heading: Hot room and rattling vents
paragraphs: We often hear, "My bedroom is hot but the rest of the house is cold," especially when a branch duct has come loose from its ceiling boot or a flex duct has been pinched in the attic. Air may still reach the register, but the reduced opening leaves the room with weak airflow.

Another common call is, "The vent is making a flapping or rattling noise." A loose metal damper, detached insulation sleeve, or unsupported flex duct can move when the blower comes on, creating a sound that seems to come from the grille or the ceiling cavity.

Some callers report dust around a supply vent, an attic smell when the AC runs, or a return grille that seems louder than before. An open return seam can draw dusty attic air into the ductwork, while a split supply duct can push air and insulation fibers into spaces around the run.

We also check vents that have stopped blowing altogether, because a collapsed flex section, a disconnected collar, and a closed or blocked damper can feel identical from inside the room. These faults require different materials and different amounts of access work, so we inspect the duct before tying the repair to a particular scope.

sections.heading: Ductwork inspection
paragraphs: We begin with a ductwork inspection that commonly takes about thirty to sixty minutes for an accessible problem. We identify the affected register and return grille, inspect the air handler connections, and follow the branch run through the attic, crawlspace, garage, or ceiling cavity where access allows.

We check flex duct for tears, compression, kinks, missing insulation, and sagging sections. At collars, boots, plenums, and takeoffs, we look for separated joints, failed mastic, loose straps, and foil tape that is no longer holding the seam. We can also measure airflow and static pressure in inches of water column when the symptom points to a restriction or a larger duct issue.

On an accessible visit, we can usually reconnect a loose run, secure a collar, seal a reachable seam with mastic, replace damaged straps, or cut out and replace a short split section of flex duct. We verify airflow at the register after the repair and check that insulation covers the repaired section.

If the damaged run is buried beneath decking, passes through a tight ceiling cavity, has several failed branches, or needs a larger section rebuilt, we explain the route and schedule the additional ductwork work separately. A replacement section may also need to be ordered when the existing duct diameter, insulation rating, or metal fitting is not available for the visit.

sections.heading: Attic access, flex duct, and collars
paragraphs: We look first at access because an exposed duct in a walkable attic is a different repair from a run above a finished ceiling or behind stored items. A narrow attic hatch, low roof framing, wet insulation, and a long route to the damaged branch all add labor to reach the collar, boot, or split section safely.

The duct material and extent of the damage also affect the work. A loose collar may need sealing and a new mechanical connection, while crushed flex duct may need a new section, support straps, insulation, and a properly sized connector. Sheet-metal trunks, return plenums, and custom transitions can require different fittings than a standard flex run.

Older ductwork can reveal more than one weak point once the insulation sleeve is opened. If several seams have failed, a return box has deteriorated, or a branch diameter is incorrect, we explain which repair addresses the immediate airflow problem and which additional work would prevent the same loss from returning.

If a fitting or specialty duct material has to be ordered, the scope changes from a straightforward accessible repair to a return visit with the correct part. When an alteration requires a permit or inspection, we also account for the access, material, and sign-off steps involved.

sections.heading: Air handler label and attic hatch
paragraphs: Before calling, we recommend noting which room has the weak, hot, noisy, or dusty vent and whether it is a supply register or return grille. If the system is running, tell us whether air is coming from the register, whether the blower sound changed, and whether the issue affects one room or several rooms.

The model number on the air handler data plate, usually found on the blower cabinet or indoor unit, helps us understand the equipment serving the ducts. A photo of the ceiling vent, attic hatch, visible flex duct, or disconnected collar can also help us bring suitable tape, mastic, straps, and fittings.

Let us know where the attic hatch, crawlspace door, garage access, or mechanical closet is located and whether storage blocks the route to the duct run. We can be reached at (512) 635-7760, because a loose supply or return duct can keep losing conditioned air and pulling attic dust into the home while it remains open.

services.name: Thermostat Repair
services.title: Thermostat Repair | Air Conditioning Austin | Austin, TX
services.meta: Air Conditioning Austin provides thermostat repair in Austin, TX, with control checks, wiring tests, calibration, and clear next steps for home comfort.
services.blurb: Wall control diagnostics, wiring checks, and thermostat repair across Austin.

paragraphs: Older Austin homes, remodeled rooms, and properties with original wall controls often develop thermostat trouble before the rest of the cooling equipment shows an obvious fault. A thermostat can lose its temperature calibration, develop a loose wire behind the wall plate, or stop communicating with the indoor unit after a battery, power, or programming issue. We cover Austin, Rollingwood, West Lake Hills, and Lost Creek from our location on Commercial Park Dr.

A control installed in a sunny hallway can read warmer than the living room, while a thermostat near a kitchen, exterior door, or supply register can react to heat or cool air that does not reflect the rest of the house. Older mercury-style controls, programmable units, and newer Wi-Fi thermostats each use different terminals, settings, and power arrangements, so the screen alone does not identify the fault.

Thermostat repair should not wait when the wall control will not start or stop cooling correctly, because that small control is sending the command for the entire system to run, cycle, or remain off. A display setting that is merely inconvenient may be less urgent, but a thermostat that leaves the home too warm or keeps the equipment running needs a proper check.

sections.heading: Blank screen and wrong temperature
paragraphs: A blank thermostat screen is one of the most common calls. Sometimes the issue is a depleted battery, corroded battery contact, tripped power supply, or a loose common-wire connection behind the wall plate. A screen that is lit but will not respond to buttons, loses its clock, or repeatedly reconnects to Wi-Fi points to a different set of controls and power checks.

Another common report is, “The thermostat says it is cool, but the room is hot,” or “The number on the screen is not the same as the thermometer.” That can come from sensor calibration, the thermostat location, a damaged sensor, a programmed schedule, or a control signal that is not reaching the indoor equipment. We also hear about cooling that starts but shuts off too soon, a fan that runs when the thermostat is off, and a thermostat that will not switch out of one mode.

These symptoms can look nearly identical from the wall, but a battery contact, sensor, terminal, control wire, and failed thermostat are separate faults with different parts and labor involved. Looking at the display and testing the terminals is how we separate a setting issue from a component or wiring issue.

sections.heading: Control wiring diagnostic callout
paragraphs: During a thermostat diagnostic callout, we start with the wall control, the temperature setting, the operating mode, and the power source. We remove the faceplate where appropriate, inspect the R, C, Y, G, and other connected terminals, check for loose conductors or damaged insulation, and test the low-voltage control circuit. Most residential thermostat circuits use about 24 volts, and a meter reading at the thermostat helps show whether power is reaching the control and whether the call for cooling is leaving it.

We compare the thermostat reading with the room temperature, review schedules and hold settings, and check whether the indoor equipment responds when the control makes a call. A straightforward screen, battery, setting, terminal, or calibration check commonly takes 30 to 60 minutes. Battery replacement, terminal tightening, programming corrections, and a compatible thermostat replacement can often be handled on the visit when the needed part is available; concealed wiring damage, an incompatible smart control, or a special-order thermostat may need a follow-up appointment.

sections.heading: Control wiring and wall access
paragraphs: The condition and age of the thermostat matter because older controls may use terminals or mounting plates that do not match current replacements. A basic issue at the battery compartment or a loose wire at the wall plate is usually more direct than a failed internal sensor, damaged control board connection, or a thermostat that requires a specific compatible model. If the existing control has been discontinued, the replacement choice can depend on the wiring already present behind the wall.

Access also affects the work. A thermostat on an open interior wall is easier to inspect than wiring routed through a finished wall, behind cabinetry, or through a return chase. A wire that has broken inside the wall, a terminal that has overheated, or a replacement control that has to be ordered adds steps beyond a standard wall-control check. We explain which component is causing the problem and whether the repair can be completed with the parts available.

sections.heading: Model number and wall plate
paragraphs: Before calling, check the model number on the thermostat faceplate, back cover, or label behind the wall plate if it can be removed safely. Let us know which room has the control, whether the screen is blank or lit, and whether the cooling equipment is running now, running constantly, or not responding at all. The approximate age of the thermostat, the make printed on its display or housing, and a photo of the wiring terminals can help us prepare for the right type of control. Mention whether the thermostat is on a high wall, behind furniture, or near a stairwell so we know what access is involved. Call Air Conditioning Austin at (512) 635-7760 before a faulty thermostat leaves the cooling equipment cycling continuously or prevents it from turning on when the indoor temperature rises.

We take on AC repair, AC tune-up, air conditioner replacement, air conditioner installation, duct repair, and thermostat repair. We repair equipment in houses, apartments, offices, and shops, and replace air conditioners at properties throughout our service area.

A visit starts with our technician checking the thermostat, indoor unit, outdoor condenser, air filter, drain line, wiring, and refrigerant readings. We look for the source of the problem, note the condition of the equipment, and discuss findings before anybody talks about money.
